I just did a bunch of back of the envelope calculations regarding energy density of gas and graphene ultracaps.

Tricky stuff because they are measured completely differently, and everything is a range.

What I found was: Maximum energy density achieved in graphene caps (so far) is about 88 Wh per Liter

Gas is 45 MJ per Kg

45 MJ is 12500 Wh

1 L of gas weighs ~750g

1g of gas is 12.5 Wh

750g of gas (~1 L) = 9375 Wh

Now the only thing that would substantially tilt anything back towards graphene with that disparity would be efficiency. I believe electricity to an electrical motor is a LOT more efficient than burning gas in an ICE. But even so, assume gas is HALF as efficient (probably a gross exaggeration), 9375 / 2 = 4687.

4687 / 88 is 53.2, so gas is approximately 53.2x more energy dense than graphene caps by weight.

Which is a big mountain to climb, and again I doubt that electrical is DOUBLE the efficiency of ICE.
